subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUCCESSFUL LAUNCHING OF CANADIAN SATELLITE

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUCCESSFUL LAUNCHING OF CANADIAN SATELLITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday night at 11.04 p.m. Pacific daylight time the satellite Alouette, developed by the defence research board here in Ottawa, was successfully launched into orbit from Vandenberg air force base in California atop a Thor Agena rocket provided by the United States national aeronautics and space administration. This culminated three years of effort to combine applied science and technical skill by scientists here in Canada, and marks the first occasion for a space craft to be completely designed and built by a nation other than the United States or the Soviet union.
Signals from the satellite are now being received by tracking stations around the world including eight operated by NASA and two by the British, while here in Canada three defence research board stations are already receiving important data. The satellite passed over Ottawa for the first time shortly after noon on Saturday, and on subsequent passes tracking and the reception of information has been very satisfactory.
The Alouette is being called upon to carry out four experiments, three designed by the defence research board and the fourth by the national research council. One will seek the electron density distribution within a specific layer of the ionosphere; a second will determine changes in the ionosphere directly below the orbiting satellite; a third will measure cosmic radio noise, and the fourth, designed by national research council, will measure primary cosmic ray particles which are related to auroral effects and the leakage of particles in the upper atmosphere. If these experiments are completely successful, and at the moment we have every reason to believe that they will be, they will have valuable practical application to the technology of long range telecommunications both for civil and defence purposes.
Our collaboration with NASA, which includes the launching of a similar satellite in the near future, will result in a pooling of scientific data that will add much to what we already know.
The government and industrial scientists and engineers who have contributed to this project have acquired new experience, knowledge and skills which will improve Canada's international stature and industrial competitive position in an expanding technological field. Valuable experience has also been gained by Canadian firms which have participated in this project, in particular the de Havilland Aircraft Company in Toronto which developed the unique antenna system for the satellite and which has already received large United States orders for similar antennae and expects more orders to come. Another Canadian contractor, R.C.A. Victor Company Limited of Montreal, has a firm prospect for United States orders for telemetry transmitters of the type developed for the satellite.
This has been an outstanding Canadian achievement which could not have been successful without the close co-operation and support of officials in the United States, industry here in Canada and, in particular, without the earnest endeavours of all who participated in this project within the defence research board.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUCCESSFUL LAUNCHING OF CANADIAN SATELLITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house would like to join with the government in congratulating all those who have participated in the successful launching of the Alouette satellite. It is indeed an outstanding achievement. It is a demonstration of the high quality of Canadian scientists and of their capabilities and endeavours in this collective achievement. It is also an indication of the successful teamwork on the part of government scientists working closely with those of private industry.
We also appreciate the excellent co-operation of our American neighbours, and particularly of the United States air force, in putting the satellite in orbit. We congratulate all those who participated in any way in the project on their magnificent achievement.

Mr. Speaker, we in the Social Credit party would like to join in extending our sincere congratulations to those whose efforts have led to the accomplishment to which we are now referring. It is an example to the world of international co-operation in the peaceful development of modern science, and shows the progress which can be made and to what extent we can go forward in this field.

On the order: Government notices of motion:
September 27-The Prime Minister:
That a humble address be presented to Her Majesty the Queen in the following words:
To the Queen's Most Excellent Majesty:
Most Gracious Sovereign:
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the Senate and Commons of Canada in parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty, praying that you may graciously be pleased to cause a measure to be laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom to be expressed as follows:
An act to amend the British North America Act, 1867.
Whereas the Senate and House of Commons of Canada in parliament assembled have submitted an address to Her Majesty praying that Her Majesty may graciously be pleased to cause a measure to be laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom for the enactment of the provisions hereinafter set forth:
Be it therefore enacted by the Queen's most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in this present parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same, as follows:
1. Section ninety-four A of the British North America Act, 1867 is hereby repealed and the following substituted therefor:
27507-3-4J
Proposed Legislation
"94A. It is hereby declared that the parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to
(a)	old age pensions, and
(b)	pensions and other benefits incidental to„ or conducive to the better operation and administration of, a scheme of old age pensions,
but no law made by the parliament of Canada under the authority of this section affects the operation of any law enacted by the legislature of a province in relation to any of the matters specified in paragraphs (a) and (b) of this section."
2. This act may be cited as the British North America Act, 1963, and the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1962, and this act may be cited together as the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1963.

CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN RErLY
The house resumed from Friday, September 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gordon Chaplin for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I desire first of all to observe the traditional and worthy custom-at some times easier to follow than at others-of congratulating the mover (Mr. Chaplin) and seconder (Mr. Vincent) of the address in reply. Today the task is an easy one because both hon. members performed their task in a way which was creditable to themselves and to their party. They must, I think, have made an impression on all members of the house because of the constructive nature of their contributions.
I may perhaps be pardoned for saying an additional word about the mover because of the fact that his father was so long associated in such an honourable and important way with our deliberations as a member of the house. As I have ventured to tell the hon. member already, I think his father would have been very proud and happy if he had been here last Friday.
The first business of this parliament once the formalities have been completed-and it has taken a little time to complete these formalities this afternoon-must be to decide in accordance with our constitutional and democratic rights whether the minority government now in office has the confidence of this House of Commons. In the present circumstances-and I emphasize "in the present circumstances"-such a motion takes precedence over other business, as it has done in the past in similar circumstances. For this purpose it is the duty and the privilege of the official opposition to move a motion which will make that decision possible. That duty is obvious. Indeed, it is inescapable when nearly 63 per cent of the voters in this country have declared in a recent election that they have no confidence in this government, in its policies and in its leadership.
If there were to be any surprise expressed, it would be not that we are following the course I have indicated but that we did not intend to follow it having regard to the repudiation of the government on June 18 and the stand taken by this party in the recent election campaign. A motion of no confidence having been moved, it becomes the duty of every member of this newly elected house to vote for or against it. If the decision results in the defeat of the government then there will be a dissolution and a general

election at which time the people will make a final decision-one that they almost made last June 18. On June 18 they made their negative decision. Next time they will make their positive decision. Since when has a move to give the House of Commons an opportunity- and an obligation-to declare its position in regard to confidence in a minority government been wrong, or playing politics? Since when has a declared willingness to accept an appeal to the people, which a decision against the government would produce, become something to be condemned? Since when has it become responsible to declare confidence in a government in which you have many times before, during an election campaign and afterwards, declared you have no confidence? I may say that contrary to some allegations made in forceful terms, there will be none of our members removed from the house when the vote is taken. We do not aspire to hold the record for absentee membership in this house.
If the house should reject our motion of non-confidence-and I hope it will not-then the government has a mandate at least to introduce its legislative and other proposals- a mandate which it has not got now-and each of those proposals will be considered by this party on its merits in exactly the same way as if the government had a clear majority in this house.
That is our position. It is in this spirit that in due course we shall support this position of non-confidence by moving an amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Whatever decision any other party in this house may have reached, we have no confidence in this government, nor has the country any confidence in this government. Its record over the past five years, together with its record over the recent election campaign and since, has been condemned, and not only by us. That record surely abundantly justifies and even demands the stand we are taking. Nor is there anything in the speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, which would warrant a change in our views. Quite the contrary, as the other two opposition parties themselves admit.
The leader of the Social Credit party is reported in the press to have said in Ottawa on September 26 that, to move a vote of non-confidence in the government-and remember, this is a government which was opposed in an election by nearly 63 per cent of the voters-is political and parliamentary irresponsibility.
I hear comment on the other side, but such comments are not made in the same volume as they were in the old days, when hon. members opposite erupted like volcanoes; and it is noticeable that some of the chief erupters are no longer with us.
The Address-Mr. Pearson
Here is what the co-leader of the Social Credit party said a few weeks earlier than his leader's statement, as reported in the press. On August 8, at Timmins, he said:
I have fought against Diefenbaker outside parliament. I will not fight for him inside it. The country needs a stable government. I would like to see one too. The quicker we have another election, the quicker we will have such a government.
Those are true words, Mr. Speaker. That kind of statement, therefore, makes us on this side just a little sceptical about the subsequent reasons for criticizing us for bringing forward a motion of no confidence which, if the house votes for it, will bring that stable government about.
Mr. Speaker, a vital requirement for national progress and stability in a democracy is confidence in the government of the day. The people showed last June that they did not have such confidence in this government. The government record, both before and since, shows that it does not deserve such confidence. Will it help Canada if, by voting confidence in this minority government, we reject this verdict of the people, ignore the records, and deny the validity of positions previously taken, and declared by those who took them to be in the national interest? There can be no stability in government when over any substantial period the party in power cannot ordinarily command a majority in the House of Commons. Smaller parties or groups may like it this way on occasion, because it might give them an influence they would not otherwise have. But the principle remains valid surely, that a party, either by itself or by arrangement for continuing support from some other party, should be able to count on the support of a majority of the members of this house. Otherwise a government would have to tailor all its legislation and all its proposals to the requirements and to the support of any smaller group on which its life depends. Now, the Prime Minister- and it is always nice to quote the Prime Minister in these situations, and I must say that he lends himself to quotation-
What about yourself?

I know the Prime Minister has been looking through my speeches too. I have no doubt of that, and he has a great quantity of helpers working on this subject. But I did not need any help to look for some of his quotations. The Prime Minister has recognized in the past the instability of minority government, indeed the impossibility of minority government. He did that, of course, when his fortunes were in the ascendant. On January 25, 1958, at a press conference in Winnipeg, he referred to the impossibility of his government carrying on in its minority

The Address-Mr. Pearson position-and this, remember, shortly alter a time when he had been successful at the polls and had been assured of the co-operation of the official opposition, which I confess with sorrow had been defeated in that election. And yet even in these favourable circumstances for the Prime Minister, he is reported by the press of that day as having said:
This condition of affairs-
That is, government by a minority.
-cannot continue if Canada is to have that effective parliamentary government it needs.
Then he added that his government "lacks the freedom to act", but presumably he has found that freedom now. He also said that that minority government, in those favourable circumstances, was forced into "the predicament of day-to-day planning, instead of the long term planning" that the realm required. Then he added these words, which I quote again from the report:
The experience of the past few months has proved to me that it is impossible for a government to operate efficiently in a minority position.
Well, the Prime Minister seems to feel very differently now. In a much more difficult minority position, and after a defeat at the polls, not a victory, the Prime Minister now asks for the right to carry on inefficiently. Some of us also remember those words of the Prime Minister uttered in this house on that day, February 1, 1958, when with histrionics, and dramatics he dissolved parliament; and for him it was a very fortunate dissolution indeed, more fortunate than the one last spring. On page 4200 of Hansard for that day he is reported as saying:
The present government is supported by 113 members out of a total of 265. Its position as a minority government has become intolerable. No other party or group in this house can possibly form a government; ... The only way in which the present situation can be effectively resolved is by the course I am about to announce.
That course was dissolution, followed by a general election, before he was ever defeated in the house on any issue.
Then the Prime Minister continued in this house in the following words:
No hon. member will suggest that a situation in which a government can depend upon the support of only a minority of the members of this house is a satisfactory situation, or one that could he expected to continue long.
Well, we will give the Prime Minister the chance and help him realize now that expectation, that this is not a situation which should be allowed to continue long. It has already continued since June 18.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the composition of this house as a result of the election of June 18 certainly shows that we have a government possessing the confidence only of a minority

of this house, and of a minority of the country as well. This new parliament, I do not need to tell you, is very different from the old; though from what we have heard this afternoon from the ministerial benches the government already seems to have forgotten that fact. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) had this to say on the very eve of the last election, and this has a bearing on the changed composition of the house. I quote from the broadcast he made on June 14, I think it was. He will remember it.
As I travel about and meet people, I find this. They know how to separate wheat from chaff.
Then he went on:
And the chaff of five years is being spread asunder.
That is very true indeed, because in the recent separation of wheat from chaff the Conservative government lost more members, 86, than any party has lost in any election in our history-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: We had more to lose.
-and that after less than five years in office.
We had more to start with.

On the other hand, this party over here, I am proud, happy and comforted to say, has doubled its membership from 50 to 100 with the largest percentage of the popular vote. I call that fact to the attention of the Prime Minister who has been stating otherwise. I know this cannot be very comforting for my hon. friends opposite to listen to and I know their minds are going back to the old days when they had 204 or 205 shouting supporters to howl us down whenever we made statements of this kind in the house. But those days are ended.
You will never shout us down.

The Conservative defeat was catastrophic but I would be the first to admit that it was indecisive because they are still in office. They are still in office, Mr. Speaker, after losing 86 members, but they will not be in office much longer. This defeat must, I think, have been all the more surprising, indeed, perhaps shocking to them, in view of certain factors during the election. I am going to mention some of them and one or two I am going to go into in considerable detail. There is their success, for instance, in concealing the financial crisis from the electors and the really desperate effort they made and the

tactics they followed in which the bill of rights became a Conservative campaign document-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It certainly was not a Liberal one.
-in which communism was put on our side to help their side-
You should know.
By the former minister of finance too.

-by ministers who should have known better. Let us look at my statement about concealment of the financial situation from the electors, which was a very important factor in the election itself. Within a few hours after the election of June 18 this minority government had to deal with a financial and exchange crisis which had been concealed from the electors by what can only be termed a major political fraud, fraud by concealment and misrepresentation of the situation. Let us look at the evidence, and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) figures largely in the evidence.
The farmers certainly knew where the "fraud" was.
The evidence on this very important point provides one of the strongest reasons for voting no confidence in this government. Who deceived whom?
That is the question.
That is the question all right and I will answer the question.

You will be sorry.
The Address-Mr. Pearson know whether there is any particular significance to be attached to that kind of transition from finance to justice-boasted in his budget speech on April 10 and right through the election campaign that the nation's finances were in wonderful shape. He scorned the very idea of devaluing and pegging the dollar before May 2. We had the minister's jeers and the even more violent reaction of the Prime Minister when we in the Liberal opposition talked about pressure on the dollar, the depreciation of our reserves, the foreign help that had to be secured and the financial dangers that were certainly ahead. Yet the Prime Minister in that broadcast of June 14 assured the country that all was well and that we, who said otherwise and unfortunately proved to be right-that was our crime-were besmirching the good name of Canada for political reasons.
You have been doing it for five years.

Let us see who was besmirching whom. Then we have the Minister of Agriculture. On June 20, after the election was over, everybody but the minister apparently knew what the situation was. Even his colleagues knew because it was possible for them to talk candidly about what had happened; but not the Minister of Agriculture. On June 20 after the election and four days before the emergency austerity program was announced he made the incredible statement that "there is no crisis that anyone can point a finger at".
Every indicator was moving up.

The Minister of Agriculture seems a little nervous this afternoon, a little agitated, shall we say.
The farmers certainly
threshed you.

I beg him to be calm. The Prime Minister in his television broadcast on June 14 had this to say, and I quote from the text of that broadcast as it was circulated:
We have given you the facts.
This was June 14.
We have given you the facts. We have bared the record. We have concealed nothing and shaded nothing.
What was the version of the facts, Mr. Speaker, which on this occasion the Prime Minister said they had given to the people of Canada, concealing nothing and shading nothing? What was their version of the facts with respect to the developing crisis? The minister of finance of that day, who is Minister of Justice (Mr. Fleming) now-I do not

There were a great many people in this country and abroad, not interested in politics, not even interested in the Canadian election, who had pointed out and emphasized the same dangers and called attention to the same results that would happen if something were not done about it.

Why should they have ignored the reassuring statements of the Prime Minister? This was a very great tribute to me indeed. I had no idea that I had the power to influence national and international financial interests. It is very flattering indeed.
The Prime Minister's thesis, about which we are going to hear later on, I suppose, is also affected and made slightly ridiculous by the fact that a large percentage of the loss, as we know now, was due to Canadians moving their money out of Canada. The Minister of Agriculture, particularly, may have had something to do with this. In fact, he probably had a lot to do with it. He was a privy councillor who had taken the oath of secrecy, and he talked about the division of opinion inside the cabinet. How can you square the Prime Minister's thesis with the fact that the movement out accelerated alarmingly after the election, when it became clear that the voting had not displaced the government or put us in.

The fact that our exchange difficulties were so greatly increased after the election, during those two or three days before action was taken, is the most damning indictment of the policy of the government and its reputation in this field that any government could receive. Had there been a different result to the election there would not have been that flight from the Canadian dollar after June 18. The government's explanation of the nature, cause and timing of the dollar crisis in June is false to the point of being nonsensical but, as we shall probably be given it again by the Prime Minister and his colleagues during the course of this debate, it is necessary for me to put the facts on the record and show how we got into this position. That I propose to do in very considerable detail.
We on this side of the house in the previous parliament repeatedly pointed out that a financial crisis was developing and that it was mainly-although we never attempted to say it was solely-due to government mismanagement. Perhaps I may be permitted to quote what I said in the budget debate on April 17, 1962, which may be the last budget for which this government will be responsible. I said, as recorded in Hansard of that date at page 3073:
The situation now is that instead of buying United States dollars in order to get our reserves up and get our dollars down he is selling United States dollars in order not to depress but to support the Canadian dollar, to stop it from going down too far.
It is going down and it may go down too far because of loss of confidence in that dollar. One reason for that loss of confidence, in addition to certain ambiguous statements by the minister, was the shameless Coyne affair and the effects it had abroad.
This operation of the minister which was to bolster our reserves, has cost our reserves about $350 million in the first three months of this year. I can only describe that, Mr. Chairman, as muddled manipulation of our dollar.
That was done by a government which, only a short time before, had refused in this house to accept any responsibility for monetary policy.
During the election campaign we repeated our warnings and said the country was already facing a dollar crisis. The Prime Minister and his colleagues denied the existence of this crisis and they accused us of falsifying the facts. They claimed that the devaluation announced in May was a deliberate, planned attempt by the government to promote expansion. We said such a decision had been imposed upon the government by necessity and was another undeniable sign of the crisis.
Anyone who knew anything about the subject, and that must have included some members of the government but certainly not the Minister of Agriculture, must have known what was happening and why it was happen-
The Address-Mr. Pearson ing. The reason for this situation into which we got ourselves unnecessarily goes back through the whole period of the last parliament when this government was in office.
The stagnation experienced since 1957, and our chronic trade deficits, were bound to weaken the external value of the Canadian dollar; but until fairly recently that underlying weakness was met by a net inflow of capital, so that the Canadian dollar remained at a relatively high premium with respect to the United States dollar while our official holdings of gold and United States dollars also remained at a fairly constant level. That was true until the end of 1960; but in December, 1960, the value of the Canadian dollar began to decline slowly until June 1961 when it was about par with the American dollar.
What happened to produce that trend? It was due to three steps in particular taken by this government. First, the non-resident withholding taxes were sharply increased in the so-called "baby budget" in December, 1960, which contributed to discouraging capital coming in from abroad.
Second, the Minister of Finance and the Bank of Canada at that time strongly advised the provinces, the municipalities and other potential Canadian borrowers not to borrow in the United States.
Third, as we learned only in June, 1961, from the former governor of the bank of Canada, the Minister of Finance, in December, 1960, began to manipulate in secret the exchange rate and to buy United States dollars.
Those three factors, for which the government is responsible-and nobody else-fully account for the slow decline in the value of the Canadian dollar which occurred between November, 1960, and June, 1961. Then in July, 1961, the Canadian dollar suddenly dropped by about three cents to 96J cents in terms of the U.S. dollar. This was the beginning of the rot; and two factors, directly connected with the government, account for that sudden change for which it must take full responsibility.
I have mentioned one already. It is impossible to overestimate the Coyne affair, that sorry and shameful episode which caused a great deal of concern not only in our own country but abroad. It did more than any other single thing to destroy financial confidence in our country. Indeed it has been called devaluation by slander.
The second factor was that the Minister of Finance in his budget speech of June, 1961, finally decided to admit publicly that he was manipulating the exchange rate in order to bring about "a significant discount", although he refused to tell us what he meant by

1961,	our holdings of U.S. dollars declined each month and that meant of course, contrary to what the minister had said, that the government was not buying but selling U.S. dollars in order to support the value of the Canadian dollar. That new policy and the minister's refusal to say what he meant by a "significant discount" were bound to cause uncertainty and a further loss of confidence on the financial market.
Then there was the huge budgetary deficit announced by the minister at that time, which was another contributing factor. It meant that all the main elements of a dollar crisis were now at work, and the government was responsible for all of them.

When the government decided to devalue at the beginning of May, the Prime Minister must surely have known that such an exceptional step was taken by necessity, as an attempt to stop the run on our reserves. He must have known that devaluation had become inevitable on that ground. But there was an election going on and the Canadian public was led to believe by the Prime Minister himself that this exceptional decision was merely part of a deliberate and planned policy to increase exports and to encourage domestic industries.
There is another factor which bears on this question. When the level of our reserves at the end of May became known and showed a further substantial decline, the Prime Minister must at that time, surely, have become convinced that devaluation had failed to stop the dollar crisis and that something else had to be done.
The government's advisers in Ottawa were certainly aware of the existence of the dollar crisis, and I am certain they discharged that responsibility of keeping the Prime Minister and the minister of finance informed of the situation even during an election campaign. When action was taken after the election, the Prime Minister and his colleagues had only four days in which to prepare an austerity program including the determination of the new tariff schedules and the negotiation of the various loans in the United States and in Great Britain. It is surely unbelievable that the austerity program could have been thought of, initiated and implemented in a period of only four days. The Prime Minister must have known before the election that such a program was being developed in order to be ready for implementation immediately after the election. For all these reasons any impartial observer must come to the only possible conclusion, namely that our dollar crisis, our financial crisis, was developing over the months and that the Prime Minister was fully aware of it long before his telecast of June 14. In that perspective, and because of the other reasons I have given, surely the statement made in that telecast was both improper and misleading.
Then came the morning after the election, after our celebration and the hon. gentleman's desolation, and the amazing about-face of the Prime Minister and his government on this issue which had been put before the electors in such optimistic and concealing ways. We suddenly realized in this country that we were facing a crisis of confidence-a real emergency. We realized we were facing difficulties which would go beyond the emergency itself-that we were facing a need for long range programs which would get to the root of the difficulties. Above all we were

facing a need for a restoration of confidence. In addition, we were facing a conference of commonwealth prime ministers.
In the light of all this, what did the government do after the election? Mr. Speaker, they told us to cool off and forget it. I can understand why they gave this advice to cool off, forget what had been said and what had been happening. The government told us, somewhat unctuously, to tighten our belts and get ready for austerity after the election. They took emergency action leading up to austerity and, of course, they shuffled what was left of the cabinet deck, adding a second senator to it. I think this is the first time since the early thirties, in Mr. Bennett's day, that we have had two senators in the cabinet. Maybe I am wrong about this, but I think I am right. It is, perhaps, a step in the reform of the Senate, but it has other implications.

It will be recalled that the hon. gentleman in question who served his country during the war in Ottawa with distinction and devotion, was one of Mr. C. D. Howe's wartime bureaucrats. He was one of those men who were trampling the liberties of the people under foot.

However, he poured scorn on these people and particularly he poured personal scorn on Liberal candidates who, he claimed, were bureaucrats in those days despite the fact that one or two whom he attacked personally had not spent their wartime years in Ottawa but were fighting overseas. However, this particular appointment has purified some of my colleagues and I am grateful for that.
The Prime Minister's reaction was an understandably happy one when the appointment was announced. He drew a parallel which, I confess, surprised me a little. He said: President Kennedy has his McNamara; I have my McCutcheon. When the Prime Minister said that, I thought we were at

least going to get a defence policy. If I am not wrong, I believe Mr. McNamara is secretary of defence in the United States government. The Prime Minister's exhilaration over this appointment was badly timed because at the time he was reported to have made that remark the house armed services committee in Washington accused Mr. McNamara on August 13 of accumulating power in a way which could lead to the disastrous erosion of military effectiveness.
We all remember that while these steps were being taken by the government, and indeed, weeks afterwards, no economic program was put forward; no parliament was called to deal with what we were told was a grave national crisis. What have they done? They should have called parliament together at the first date possible under our constitution. Imagine a man who talks so much and with such emotion about the responsibilities of parliament and the privileges of the House of Commons refusing to call parliament together at a time which he claims to have been one of national emergency after an election. They should have done what was done in 1925 and 1926 which was the only time previously when we had a minority government in a comparable situation.
Not comparable in any way.

Comparable. The year which the Prime Minister put forward as a precedent was not a precedent at all in relation either to the situation now or in 1925 and certainly 1957 did not provide a comparable situation. True, in 1957 there was a minority government but, as I have already said, the Liberals had, in effect, been defeated in that election even though no party had a majority in the house. Mr. St. Laurent recognized that by resigning, and indicated that the party which had been the most successful in the election should have a chance to implement its proposals which had, on the whole been supported by the electorate. That is the stand he took in 1957. The Prime Minister should be careful not to try to relate the circumstances in 1957 to those of 1962 to justify the course of action he has taken, because the comparison would prove embarrassing to himself and to his colleagues. The truth is that on this occasion in 1962 responsible government was mocked by the Prime Minister's refusal to summon parliament at the earliest possible moment to deal with the position in which the government found itself at a time of emergency on the eve of a prime ministers' commonwealth conference called to discuss matters of the most far reaching importance. Responsible government means, if it means anything at all, that the Queen's ministers are
The Address-Mr. Pearson responsible to the elected members of the House of Commons, and must therefore have the support and the confidence of the majority of the House of Commons before they take action.
Between sessions of any one parliament the government with a clear majority can normally, of course, count on that support; but with a minority government, that is not the case. The first such parliament elected in this situation was elected on October 29, 1925. It consisted of 117 Conservatives, 101 Liberals, 24 Progressives, and 3 Labour and Independent members. This minority government of 1925 decided to submit its fate to parliament, which was summoned at the earliest possible date after the last writ was returned on January 6. What a contrast with the course followed by this minority government, which held up parliament to the last possible minute.
There is another and very glaring contrast indeed. Mr. Mackenzie King, though not in the house, was head of a minority government, and he announced-and his government acted on the announcement-that his minority government would make no appointments, and would take no action which was not required for the routine business of government, until parliament had met and decided the question of confidence. What a contrast between that position and the one taken this summer by these paragons of parliamentary rights and parliamentary responsibilities.

No government has the right to remain in office unless it can command the support of the majority of the House of Commons. The Prime Minister, therefore, should have parliament called into session at the earliest possible date and seek a vote of confidence.
That would have been the right course for the government to take even if there had been no exceptional circumstances and no financial crisis. But in the circumstances disclosed immediately after the election, there was an additional and compelling reason for the government to take that course. Instead the government chose to take action on its own to delay to the last possible date the meeting of parliament, and to carry on in the meantime as though it had the confidence and support of parliament, making appointments to the public service, to the judiciary, to the Senate, which appointments should never have been made by the government until it had been assured that it had the support of the elected House of Commons. If the proper course had been followed, the course which would have recognized the rights of parliament, the course which was advocated so strongly by Mr. Meighen in 1926 and followed at that time by Mr. King, there would have been a debate at the earliest possible moment on the speech from the throne, when consideration could have been given to the government's austerity program, to any long range proposals which were brought in, to the situation regarding the financial crisis, as we were told it was, and to the forthcoming commonwealth meeting of prime ministers. In the midst of this situation of emergency and crisis, the question could have been decided on the vote in the light of what was required by the country in a time of emergency. But that course was rejected by the government, even though it was advocated at that time both by the Social Credit and N.D.P. parties. The government merely said: Let us cool off and forget the election. By that attitude and the attitude they have taken since, they now deny the

existence of a crisis, either financial or economic. They deny that there was any emergency that justified the calling together of parliament, and they face this parliament according to their own protestations in a very different national situation, and I will have something to say about that at eight o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, at the six o'clock adjournment I was discussing what I thought was the proper course for the government to have followed during the summer in respect of the summoning of parliament. Before I go on with that I should like to correct an inaccuracy in one of my statements this afternoon when I said there had only been two cabinet ministers in the Senate in this government and in a government in the early 1930's. It has been brought to my attention that a former minister of trade and commerce, Mr. MacKinnon, for many years a member of the House of Commons as minister of that department, was transferred to the other place and served in that other place as minister without portfolio along with the leader of the government in the Senate; so that in that sense I was inaccurate.
I feel strongly, Mr. Speaker, and I tried to express that feeling this afternoon, that parliament should have been called at the earliest possible moment this summer when we were told that we were in the midst of a financial and exchange crisis. If at that time a crisis of that kind had required special consideration by parliament and if the government had needed special support to deal with the crisis, that could have been made clear in the speech from the throne and parliament could have taken whatever action was thought desirable to meet this critical emergency. That course of calling parliament was rejected by the government.
It was said that we were merely to cool off. By that attitude, by what they have said since and by what they have included in the speech from the throne they have denied that there is any longer a situation of emergency or crisis, financial or otherwise. Certainly they have denied, by not calling parliament, that there was a situation which justified taking that action, and in doing that they have confirmed that the situation today is very different indeed now.

We meet today, Mr. Speaker, in that changed situation. We are told that the emergency program of the government has worked so successfully that the immediate crisis has been removed. When that emergency program was put into effect, when the austerity program was initiated, we on this side of the house endeavoured in the national interest to co-operate and endeavoured not to oppose it. We did not exploit it for any partisan advantage even though parliament was not to be called. No matter what we may have thought of the government's responsibility in getting us into that crisis, or of its deceit in concealing it, or of certain details in the program as such, such as import surcharges and the 6 per cent bank rate, we said no word and took no action which would interfere with the effectiveness of these emergency measures in order to give them a chance.
The newly elected Liberal members of the House of Commons met in Ottawa in caucus on June 27 and they issued this statement:
The Liberal party will co-operate in effective measures to protect the soundness of the currency. Defensive emergency measures are now essential, but they must not last beyond the emergency.
Of course, the speech from the throne tells us that the emergency is over.
In addition to meeting the financial emergency, there must be effective and constructive measures to get Canada's economy moving forward again; to restore full employment and to bring about the freest possible trade. All these things must and can be done without the sacrifice of financial stability. The necessities of an emergency program should not take our minds off this ultimate objective of an expanding economy with social progress and strong national purpose.
I myself, Mr. Speaker, as leader of the party, had said on the previous day, June 26, in a statement which I issued:
All Canadians will agree that the country needs farsighted leadership and united action to prevent further devaluation of our dollar.
That was in the light of the crisis as it had been declared. Then I went on:
Emergency measures have now been taken to this end. Everyone, including the Liberal party, will support whatever these measures can do to restore confidence in the value of our currency. Our party will judge them solely by what is best for the country.
The Prime Minister showed his appreciation of that attitude, or his lack of appreciation, by deciding not to call parliament until September 27 and in the meantime to carry on as if nothing had happened on June 18. Is it to be wondered, Mr. Speaker, that we have no confidence in this government? Apart from its record over five years of ineffectiveness, confusion and indecision, are we to vote confidence in these same men, or those 27507-3-5
The Address-Mr. Pearson of them who are left, who have been so wrong so often and whose administration of the nation's business has been so bad?
Meanwhile the government's emergency measures remain in force, according to the speech from the throne, until circumstances make their removal possible. So we cannot any longer call them emergency measures. They are now government policy. But the Liberal party has not accepted, does not accept and cannot accept these Tory measures, put forward after the election as part of an emergency program, as policy of any value for the solution of our long range economic problems. In the emergency of June after the election there was no alternative, I know, because of the mess we had got into, but to borrow from abroad, though the Prime Minister said during the election that was not his policy. There was also no choice but to take some direct action to cut our spending abroad.
The Liberal party rejects as economic policies emergency measures which will not solve our problems but may indeed make them more difficult. The tariff surcharges, for instance, reduce trade and they must go. Cuts made in public works could reduce construction and employment where it is most needed. Tight money will make it harder for Canadian industry to get Canadian capital for expansion, and that has an effect on our balance of payments position. It will make it harder for provinces and municipalities to finance necessary investments in economic and social progress.
The short term inflow of capital due to high interest rates must be replaced by foreign investment for development, not hot money, and by a sensible trade policy. Austerity measures are only of emergency value in repairing the mess created in the last five years. A return to expansion and to growth will require very different measures indeed from these emergency measures. These emergency measures, Mr. Speaker, must be temporary, especially since they are on the whole restrictionist in character and their success as emergency measures will depend on the speed with which the government can get rid of them. In an economic sense austerity, whatever moral values it may have, makes no sense with unemployment and excess unused capacity. We need, above all, stability and confidence in our future, in our destiny, in our growth. We need new jobs that can only come from growth.
Now, of course, one of the most important sources of these new jobs, an important source of employment, is trade. This brings me to a matter which is mentioned in the speech from the throne, and which has been mentioned a great deal by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his colleagues,

The Address-Mr. Pearson the commonwealth economic conference in London and the prospects arising out of that conference for increasing our trade and therefore increasing employment in Canada. I know that I have been told we have no right to criticize the Prime Minister's actions at a commonwealth economic conference. I know also that he has claimed that his objective at the conference was to protect Canadian interests, Canadian jobs, Canadian income.
Well, Mr. Speaker, of course what other purpose would the Prime Minister of Canada have in going to an international conference? Of course, we accept without question the fact that was his intention, that was his objective, that was his desire. The question, Mr. Speaker, is how did he act in order to achieve that essential and desirable objective? By what methods did he protect Canadian interests, with what understanding of the situation?
There are two ways, as I see it, and this may be an oversimplification, by which this could have been done. He could have tried to protect Canadian interests by getting the best possible terms for Canada. I am now talking about United Kingdom entry into the European common market. He could have achieved this by exerting a strong but friendly influence on the United Kingdom to that end, while accepting the creative importance of United Kingdom entry into the European common market. Alternatively, he could have protected Canadian interests-and this is what I think he tried to do-by insisting on terms that would have kept the United Kingdom out, something which in itself might have been considered to be desirable. I suggest that his tactics, his policies, were based on that latter attitude.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: Are you saying this for Washington?

That is a very intelligent remark, and it is an especially intelligent observation from the member of a government which has at last discovered the wisdom of President Kennedy's trade policy.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that the making of the British entry difficult, perhaps to the point of impossibility, was also the avowed policy of certain other members of the commonwealth. They, however, with far more at stake than Canada in terms of immediate damage to their trade, played their cards far more cleverly and secured a much better reception for their position than Canada did.
How do you know?

Someone on the other side says, "How do you know?" I quote a very good authority, the secretary of state for

commonwealth relations in the United Kingdom, who ought to know. He is quoted in a newspaper which is of unimpeachable accuracy and integrity, the Toronto Telegram. The reporter for the Toronto Telegram in London quotes the secretary of state for commonwealth relations on September 17, 1962, as follows:
That where Australia and New Zealand were constructive and helpful in trying to find ways of improving commonwealth market terms, Canadians were intransigent.
Our Prime Minister, instead of talking softly in public and negotiating strongly in private, took from the very moment of his arrival in the United Kingdom, shaky though his position was at home, an aggressive position that was not likely to be effective in securing his own asserted objective of protecting Canadian jobs and income. Immediately on arrival he made two public suggestions, one of which was certainly bound to cause a lot of controversial excitement and give great comfort to the discordant British elements of the extreme right and extreme left who for different reasons were opposing British entry into the common market. They were bound to seize on any statement of this kind that was made by the Prime Minister of Canada and use it for their own purposes.
One of these two suggestions was to the effect that there must be a second prime ministers conference before Great Britain entered the European common market. This is not reflected in the communique, although continuing consultation is reflected. The other, and far more important suggestion made by our Prime Minister on his arrival in England, concerned an alternative plan to British membership in the European common market. Once that statement was made, the Prime Minister at once became the leader of the commonwealth opposition to the United Kingdom on this issue, a position which he, most of all of those attending, should have been careful to avoid. At first, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister was a little vague and coy about his alternative plan, about which apparently no one in Ottawa knew anything. He would give it only if he were asked to give it or if the United Kingdom decided not to press for entry into the common market.
Finally, at the end of the conference, the great alternative plan was produced. Well, it proved to be neither a plan nor an alternative. However, it certainly indicated the Prime Minister had lost his faith, more than once reiterated in earlier statements, in Prime Minister Macmillan's declared promise to safeguard commonwealth interests, and that included Canadian interests, in the common market negotiations. The plan, since that time, has been politely ignored. We are now

being told-I think the Prime Minister has said it himself-that the British minister in charge of common market negotiations, the Right Hon. Edward Heath, has endorsed it. When I read that statement I was interested in the kind of endorsation Mr. Heath would give to this kind of plan, so I looked up the London Times to see exactly what he said at his press conference. This is what he said, according to the London Times. This is the great endorsation of the plan:
Although Mr. Diefenbaker's suggestion for an international conference had not been discussed, it could be read into a part of the communique . . . as could the United Nations proposal for a world conference or indeed any similar initiative.
The president of Pakistan, who was a very welcome guest of the Canadian government a few days ago, did have some very friendly things to say about the Prime Minister's plan; but the finance minister of India, speaking in Ottawa a few days later, and he was here on business, merely remarked about the Prime Minister's proposal for a world trade conference of like-minded nations that a similar proposal had been made at the United Nations and that he could see no point in "duplicating, triplicating or complicating" that earlier proposal.
The fact is, of course, that this proposal of the Prime Minister's was a last minute attempt to divert attention from the failure of his tactics in London and from the very bad reception that they had in the United Kingdom and in Canada.
In view of what happened in London perhaps it is well to remember that in diplomatic negotiations with friendly governments you make your case most effectively and strongly when you do not invite misunderstanding or create ill will. It is also perhaps well to remember the old Chinese proverb, which seems to have been forgotten: "The wise man does not use a hatchet to kill a fly on the forehead of his friend." You must also know very clearly what you are seeking, not only for the short run but for the long run. In this sense the ideals and objectives of the Prime Minister may have been beyond reproach, but his diplomacy and negotiation at London for the realization of those objectives, for the protection of Canada's real interests, were both ineffective and unsuccessful. As so often before, this government exhibited its peculiar genius for getting into quite unnecessary difficulty with its friends.
On this occasion it has followed the normal course, when these things happen, of blaming others for its own difficulties, and in particular the press which, as usual, has been inaccurate and unfair. The British press, and that is not a Canadian Liberal press, was 27507-3-5i
The Address-Mr. Pearson shameful, according to some reports from government sources, and the Canadian correspondents were misguided largely, we are asked to believe, because the Canadian delegates followed the press rules of the conference after others had broken them. Mr Speaker, are our representatives really so naive as that? All this was merely a convulsive reaction of a confused and ineffective administration when things go wrong for it, as they so often do.
So far as the Prime Minister's tactics at London were concerned, they have been condemned by a good many journalistic supporters of his own government; yet the Prime Minister now tells us he really accomplished everything he wanted to in London.
He did not sell Canada short.
He did not sell Canada at all.
That is your policy.

The Prime Minister now says everything went very well at the conference and that the atmosphere, to use his words, was "friendly and fair." His words were quoted by Mr. Richard Jackson in the Ottawa Journal, and Mr. Jackson was very close to the Prime Minister at the conference. He also said:
At no time were there bitter words as reported by clandestine sources to some newspapers. The communique showed this.
However the same Mr. Richard Jackson in his very interesting report-as his reports always are-in the Ottawa Journal of September 20, which lauded the Prime Minister's position at the conference and accepted without question, indeed with ecstatic endorsation the above statements, himself added, perhaps a little carelessly at the end of the same article, these words:
Both sides in the communique gave out with the old con-the ten days of talks had all been buddy, buddy. Thissaid Mr. Jackson
-was eyewash. Blood had been spilled.
Well, Mr. Speaker, it was not as bad as that but all who support the commonwealth of nations, this essential association of men and nations representing all races, all creeds and all continents, could not help but be disturbed by some of the implications as reported from the London meeting.
A very careful and experienced observer, Mr. Robert Duffy, reporting in the Toronto Globe and Mail on September 20 expressed this worry, and I am sure it is one which must trouble a lot of people. He wrote:
Despite the genial communique on Wednesday and benign comments on it by various prime ministers, it must be obvious to everyone that the past ten days at Marlborough House have done the commonwealth no good at all.

The Address-Mr. Pearson
He went on:
The commonwealth concept (or is it a myth?) -
These were his words, and I am sure it is not a myth:
-has in fact been perceptibly damaged-just ihow badly, and with what prospects of repair, *only the future can tell.
We must hope that this is not so and that that report is too pessimistic. But certainly It is a fact, and the London conference underlines this fact, that the nature and character of the commonwealth of nations has now changed as its composition has changed and as its membership has increased. Perhaps the old informal clubbish atmosphere of pre-world war II, and immediately after that war, when a few prime ministers sat around a table in Downing street has gone forever, and this involves problems and creates new challenges for the new commonwealth.
The case against the government's tactics and policy at the London conference takes us back to the months before that conference, to the government's general attitude to the development of the European economic community, and to Britain's possible membership in that community with all that that might mean for the commonwealth and the world. That attitude on the other side of the house has shown, from the very beginning, an amazing unawareness of the historic significance of what was taking place on the continent of Europe, a significance which is as political as it is economic.
When the possibility of Great Britain joining the common market first arose a few years ago, and when that possibility was brought to the attention of the government by the opposition in this house-and the record of Hansard is clear on that point- it was shrugged off by the government as unlikely, if not impossible, or at least not worth talking about. When that reaction was shown by events to be wrong, then the next reaction was one of carping and negative criticism, expressed at times in terms that were not very friendly to the possibility of this change taking place.
Then we have the recent London conference, where the Canadian representatives adopted an attitude that ill became a government with the record of this government in respect of trade with the United Kingdom. The whole record of its trade relations with the United Kingdom was such as would have made it only decent that we should have been at least careful regarding how we would take our stand in London to protect Canadian trading interests.
That record is a revealing one of fine words. Oh, yes. Mr. Speaker, it is a record of many

fine words which, as one British member of parliament put it, "buttered no parsnips". The house knows that record and I am not going to go into it in any detail this evening. We know it from August, 1957, the fiasco of the 15 per cent diversion offer. It did not fool us on this side, but it apparently fooled the British for a short time, because in response to this 15 per cent diversion offer they made, through Mr. Thornycroft, who was then chancellor of the exchequer, an offer on behalf of the United Kingdom to help bring about the promised diversion in the only way it could be brought about, by eliminating all British tariffs on Canadian goods if Canada would reciprocate. We know what happened to that. It was ignored; it was rejected by being ignored.
We know what followed that

an increase of duties against certain British imports. We know during 1960 about the warnings of the minister of finance of that day, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) uttered as to the dangers that would come from Great Britain joining the European common market, referred to by the Minister of Agriculture in Vancouver as merely "a rich man's club". That was his interpretation of this historic European development.
We remember in August, 1960 how the minister of finance in Ste. Adele, Quebec, could hardly disguise his threats of retaliation if the United Kingdom should join ECM, and we remember-

I would like to read what The Economist, which is a highly regarded and most respected business weekly, had to say about this. The Economist of London, England, in an editorial of September 8, 1962 entitled "Facing the Commonwealth" said, and I quote one paragraph from that magazine:
What the British entry into the common market ought in the long run to offer the commonwealth is a firm link with the new Europe that is now being shaped.
And, thank God, it is being shaped.
Hear, hear.
Those words are mine.

The vision of this great adventure-
The great "I am".

If the answer were to prove a negative one-
Back and front.

As I was saying:
If the answer were to prove a negative one, that would-tragically-suggest that the commonwealth has exhausted its vein of dextrous adaptability to change in the world.

What one has missed in the last ten days, from the commonwealth leaders is an understanding of the plain fact that the uniting of Europe brings a new force into the world-and that Britain's participation is the best guarantee that the force will be steered in the right direction.
If our Prime Minister had shown some understanding, some awareness of the concept of what is happening in Europe and had expressed himself along those lines in London, what he had to say about protecting Canadian trading interests might have been understood; but what he did, of course, was quite the opposite. He publicly dissociated himself from that part of the communique in which was
The Address-Mr. Pearson put the reasons for joining and the beneficial results which might be achieved by everyone in that event.

Shame.

It was denied. That is one thing you did not read.
That report Mr. Speaker, was not denied. No denial of that report appeared at the time it was made.
Yes, it did.

Oh, oh.
What right did you have to speak about Suez in the way you did?
Oh, oh.

I will be very glad indeed to speak about Suez at any time, as I have in the past, and I will be very glad to remind the Prime Minister of his attitude at that time, which would have destroyed the formation of the first United Nation's permanent force.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, there are those who say, of course, that we in the opposition have no right to criticize the tactics followed by our Prime Minister while he was in London. This government which refused to call parliament before the conference; which refused to give any information, publicly or confidentially, to anyone outside cabinet about the policies it proposed to follow in this critical international matter; this minority government was to be immune from criticism and public opinion was to conclude from our silence that we approved of what was going on.

Oh, oh.
You should talk.

Mr. Gaitskell, the leader of the Labour party in England could criticize, and strongly, Prime Minister Harold Macmillan of England, but I must not criticize the Prime Minister of Canada.
The limits of misrepresentation of the criticism we did make were reached by the local Conservative newspaper which claims that we Liberals are taking the position, in our criticism, that Canada's trade policy should be determined by Whitehall and by some bureaucrats in Brussels without any Canadian voice at all.
Hear, hear. That is your position.

"Hear, hear", says the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fulton). Well, that criticism is false to the point of absurdity. What matters is the kind of Canadian voice; what it says, and how it says it. There was a Canadian voice at Accra-but none at Brussels-shrill in its criticism of the United Kingdom, talking about this being the end of the commonwealth, the slippery slope. There was a Canadian ministerial voice publicly and unfairly berating the British government for not supplying a report of meetings with ECM negotiators, although the information had already been provided in a full precis of the report. There was a Canadian ministerial voice belittling the great move toward European unity as the formation of a rich man's club. There was a Canadian voice shouting about a 15 per cent diversion of our imports from the United States to the United Kingdom while rejecting British initiative as to how this could be done in the interests of both our countries.
That is the kind of Canadian voice we have been hearing. It is the kind of Canadian voice we want to hear no more. One result of the tactics adopted by the Prime Minister and some others in London is that they have tried to force the British government into a position where it would have to make a choice between the commonwealth and the common market.
That is completely false.
There is no other deduction to be drawn from the stand taken which was that Britain must make a choice between the commonwealth and the common market.

speechtext: Rubbish.

No.
That is my statement and I stand by it.
You'll fall by it.

In these tactics they may have isolated the commonwealth from the ideal of European unity with Britain and from the idea of an Atlantic regional economic bloc which could be expanded by the operation of the most favoured nation clause to include all other free countries. Of course, it is the duty of the Canadian government to seek the best terms it can as the United Kingdom seeks to join the European common market. But by the great doubt thrown on the whole idea of Britain joining the ECM a heavy, unwise and unnecessary responsibility has been taken which may have harmful and unhappy results for us all.
If the United Kingdom does not join the common market, will that be in the best interests of Canada? Is it to our interest to see a European common market with the United Kingdom outside, dividing free and western Europe into two groups? Would it help us if the common market is deprived of British experience, British wisdom and British pressure to follow non-discriminatory and expansionist trade relations with the rest of the world? Will it help us if we hinder the development of a strong Great Britain as a market for our goods by insisting that the price for entry into the common market must be the entire preservation of a system of commonwealth preferences already greatly eroded since 1932? If the British do not succeed in entering the common market, has this government any plan to deal with the resulting situation except its world conference proposal? If the United Kingdom government proposes a commonwealth common market arrangement, should they not be able to get into Europe, what would be the attitude of our government to that?
What is yours?
For a few short weeks you are still the government.

Tell us.
