If the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) and the Minister of Public Works-
I have not been saying a thing.

True, the minister has not said a word and I have not said he has, but I am saying that if he and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fulton), and other ministers, wish to ascertain a sensible attitude to this question, let them read the statement made by the hon. gentleman's deputy in Vancouver. There is no doubt that Britain's entry into the ECM will confront us with problems in this country. Britain's rejection by the ECM would confront us with greater problems, so the urgent task at the commonwealth meetings in London was not to patch up the old system, not to try to make this choice between the common market and the commonwealth, but to begin a new structure of commonwealth trade within the pattern of a new trading world. Britain can gain political and economic strength by full partnership in Europe while remaining the heart and centre of the commonwealth, but a declining Britain will never mean a stronger commonwealth. There have been few greater challenges to statesmanship than the relationship we should all adopt to these European developments. If that challenge was not met in London, that was due in large part to the negative and shortsighted attitude taken by the Canadian government which over recent years has had nothing constructive to propose and no leadership to give.
Hon. members ask: What would you do? We have put this on the record in the House of Commons ever since 1959. We would have accepted as a desirable objective Great Britain's accession to the European common market and we would have gone to work at once to see how we could have associated ourselves with that move. That could have been done by showing some understanding and sympathy for the United States freer trade initiative and by trying to work with the United States and with the European common market and the United Kingdom so that the benefits of any agreements, through the most favoured nation clause might apply to all our friends as well. We should not be dragging hopefully behind the Kennedy program, which the Prime Minister has now

The Address-Mr. Pearson discovered, or throwing road blocks in the way of the United Kingdom's desire to move across the channel.
There is, of course, a very important connection between trade and jobs, and the most important need of the Canadian people at the present time is jobs. The most important task before any parliament is to find employment for the Canadian people. We have heard a great deal of complacent talk from this government about employment. This complacency reached its peak, of course, just before June 18. On June 14 the Prime Minister claimed in that famous television broadcast:
Full employment is now about to take place.
This was in June.
In this month of June we may well reach that long-Iooked-for goal of virtual full employment. It will certainly be achieved, as I see it, in July or August.
Mr. Speaker, we now have the figures to set beside the Prime Minister's vision. Unemployment in June: 301,000. That is not bad, and I am glad to say that it was an improvement over the previous June. It was not as bad as the previous June, because it was then 370,000. But, Mr. Speaker, 301,000 people were out of work even in June. Is that what the Prime Minister means by full employment? Is that his "long-looked-for goal"? Will he tell the Canadian people that his idea of full employment is to have two or almost three times as many people looking for jobs as there used to be before his day? Will he admit that? He had better look up the figures, because he will have to admit it.
How many were there?

I will put the figures on record, seeing that they are being challenged now across the aisle. Will the Prime Minister admit, when he told the electorate in June that the unemployment problem was "licked", and that we will certainly have full employment in July or August, that he was wrong again in that prediction? In June, Mr. Speaker, it was inconceivable that we would have full employment this year. But this was before the election. Economists can argue about the details, but certainly we do not have full employment when in the summer 4 per cent of our workers do not have jobs. That has been the situation this summer, and according to the government's own statistics it is equivalent to an unemployment level of 6 per cent on the average through the year. In the Liberal years from 1946 to 1957 the average was 3 per cent; and in the summer months it was generally below 2 per cent.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, this wonderful year, this year the Tories are so proud of, except in an electoral sense, is twice as bad for unemployment as an average Liberal

The Address-Mr. Pearson year. Well, Mr. Speaker, there was then no shred of evidence for saying, when the Prime Minister spoke in June, that we would have full employment in any true sense this summer. That statement was inconceivable to any responsible person. I invite the Prime Minister when he speaks to give us one of the only two possible explanations. Either he was wrong and he knew that he was wrong; or what he means by full employment is not what the Canadian people mean. It is what anyone else would call a serious level of unemployment. In June, 1957, let me remind the Prime Minister, there were 177,000 unemployed men and women in Canada. Five years later he said that he had reached the "long-looked-for goal", and we have 301,000 unemployed. Perhaps that is progress and achievement. But that was the June figure. In fairness to the Prime Minister, I must add, and I have repeated these words, that he only "thought" we would get full employment in June; but two months later he was sure there would be full employment. And so he told the Canadian public, again on television during this speech made, I think, at Brantford on June 13, and he was a little more personal about it. He got a little more personal towards the end of the election. These were his words:
Pearson and Martin will find out that in July and August we will have the lowest unemployment total in five years.
That is not much of a standard, Mr. Speaker. The five years are Tory years, and the standards are pretty low; but even so, when July and August came, Pearson and Martin did not find out what the Prime Minister told the electors we would find out. In August 280,000 people were without jobs. Even in the Tory years, the five years, there were ten previous months when unemployment had not been as bad as that.
For the month of July the Prime Minister was even further from the mark, because the unemployment figure of 308,000 was more than it had been at twelve earlier Tory dates. But of course, Mr. Speaker, the comparison to be made is not between one Tory month and another, inaccurate though that comparison has been. The comparison is between the situation in these last five years and what it was before this government came into office. The Prime Minister talks now about full employment, that he has "licked" unemployment. He said that we would have full employment in July and August, when it is more than twice as bad, nearly three times as bad, as it was in the summer of 1956.
Mr. Speaker, I direct this question to members of all parties of this house, and I ask them to consider it in their hearts and in their consciences when they come to vote on this amendment: How can we in Canada prosper with a government that thinks that
300,000 unemployed in midsummer is something to boast about? How can we meet the needs of the Canadian people with a government that says that we have full employment, when 300,000 men and women are looking for work in summer? How can we have confidence in a government which seems to think that a summer unemployment figure of 300,000 is good enough for the Canadian people?
I thought you admitted that it was 280,000?
The minister is obviously a little disturbed and a little agitated about it.

I was just trying to be
accurate.
Not knowing what these figures are, you now contradict what the Prime Minister of this country said during the election.
Oh, oh.

The speech from the throne talks in glowing terms about 200,000 new jobs that have been created; 200,000 are to be created every year. Well, Mr. Speaker, the annual increase in the labour force during the last year was just about 200,000. Is that the objective that we are to achieve? Is that our goal? Is that our target-to create enough new jobs to take care of people coming on to the labour force, but to do nothing about chronic unemployment? With only 200,000 new jobs a year, that is exactly what must happen. Our real need is not a million new jobs in five years; it is a million jobs, as I have said more than once in this house, in four years. That is what we will have to find in order to get back to full employment; not to full employment as some theoretical abstraction, but to the level of employment which was reached under Liberal administration when we did have full employment.
Mr. Speaker, the most urgent problem before us at the present time is the creation of enough jobs to take care of the men and women coming on to the labour force, and to liquidate this problem of chronic unemployment. For that purpose we need action. We need a positive program of constructive policies, instead of the Tory leftovers in the speech from the throne.
At this time I can give only some part of the program that we are going to put forward, and I will leave other parts to be filled in by my colleagues during this debate, if indeed the debate goes on.
It has not started yet.

What we need first and foremost is action for employment. How can we in Canada create the jobs that will give the unemployed a fresh start? How can we provide for the growing number of young people who are leaving our schools and colleges? How can we provide for them the opportunities they ought to have and deserve? How do we get more jobs, better jobs, secure jobs?
For these purposes there are three main steps that a Liberal government will take. We put these forward before, but in those days with the massive majority opposite no attention whatever was paid to them. They were not even debated. They were howled down when they were not ignored. First, we must have more construction, and this has some bearing on tight money. This means, of course, that our construction industry must not be strangled by the present tight money. We must provide Canadian capital for the work that needs to be done, and the biggest area of construction that is being starved today falls within the responsibility of the municipal governments. They cannot borrow at reasonable interest rates and the burden of the municipal taxes is already very heavy indeed. In other words, municipalities cannot pay for the great amount of construction and development work that needs to be done, and it surely makes every kind of economic sense to do the work rather than to have people unemployed, not producing and having to be supported without earning.
New streets, new bridges, new sidewalks, storm sewers and sewage systems, expanded water supplies, new housing, urban redevelopment-all these things need to be done and must be done. They call for an intensive effort by all Canadians and with every level of government in Canada cooperating. The contribution of the Liberal party in a Liberal program to meet this challenge is a national plan for municipal development. It will be carried out, of course, by agreement and in co-operation with the provinces, with the three levels of government working together to promote sound development where it is needed, where Canadians live and where they need jobs.
For that purpose, Mr. Speaker, we will set up, in consultation and agreement with the provinces and municipalities, a municipal loan fund. A municipality will be able to come to the fund for projects which it cannot finance at reasonable rates in today's tight money market. This is nothing new on our side. We have been putting this forward for five years and perhaps now the people on the other side will pay some attention. Of course, it will have to be done in co-operation with the 27507-3-6
The Address-Mr. Pearson provinces and the approval of the provinces will be required, but provided it does have that approval this is something that can be done and should be done. I appeal to the Prime Minister and the government to forget their past ignoring of this particular problem and to do something to co-operate in putting this kind of thing into effect. It seems to me it is more important to put men to work in the municipalities in construction jobs with federal help-and I state this to the Prime Minister-than it is to rake up the old coals of Suez.
Oh, oh.
That will help a lot, Mr. Speaker, but it will not do everything. I know hon. gentlemen opposite are having a hard time taking all this in.
A hard time taking it seriously.

Here is another measure that perhaps may appeal to them, although they seem to jeer at these proposals to put people to work. Having made such a colossal failure of their own proposals in the past they do not take easily to proposals made by anybody else that might succeed if everybody would co-operate to make them succeed.
Through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation we would provide capital grants with an extension of the federal share of expenditures for slum clearance and urban renewal. For important development projects, especially in areas particularly needing new development, we will supplement municipal loans with federal grants.

Where have you been all these
years?
I have been watching this government for the last few years do none of these things.
Oh, oh.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, these are the important measures which, if put into effect, could do something to cure this economic evil of unemployment. What it adds up to is this: We will make it possible for the municipalities to have a massive increase in construction. We know this is going to cost money but, Mr. Speaker, it will be an investment expenditure by the government, an investment which will more than pay for itself in increased employment and incomes for Canadians. Half a billion dollars of construction means the equivalent of a year's work, I am informed, for 100,000 men, and their employment in turn would mean stimulation for a great deal of other businesses.
Well, that is part of our plan for more jobs, for better places for Canadians to live and work. Our point No. 2 is the promotion of new industries. Now, the government has talked a lot about that in the last five years, what they were going to do to promote new industries. However, they have talked more

than they have acted. We need new industries, especially in the depressed areas, and to achieve that purpose we will have to use, to a greater extent than we have before, the industrial development bank to provide special credit facilities for those areas. I know, Mr. Speaker, that this is in the speech from the throne. However, this kind of thing has been in the speech from the throne for the last four years. The government puts it in the speech, then they do not do anything about it.

We have to work with industry on a co-operative basis. The government has to gain knowledge of the conditions of each industry in order to work out arrangements to achieve this objective. One instance, and perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) will be interested in this, is the automobile industry. Last year we imported $300 million worth of automobile parts into this country. This represents the equivalent of between 40,000 and 50,000 jobs. Is it really impossible, Mr. Speaker, to produce more thoroughly Canadian cars? Can we afford to allow this situation to continue? Can we not do what other countries have done?
Raise tariffs.
It is not a question of raising tariffs at all; that is the only thing that occurs to my friends.
Read your own report.

Sweden, which is smaller than we are, has a successful automobile industry, and has an industry which is exporting automobiles to this country. Is that due to Swedish tariffs? Even the French and German industries have a domestic market which is not larger than ours. Surely, Mr. Speaker, in this country we have enough initiative and intelligence, enough co-operative effort with industry left to bring about that kind of situation in Canada. By going through our whole economy, industry by industry, we can get more things made in Canada without becoming a protectionist country. If the government wants to know how this can be done in Canada perhaps, let them not only read the Bladen report, let them do something about the Bladen report.
Three years old.
Yes, it is about three years old.
On the shelf, dusty.

The Liberals have come out for a big increase in tariffs tonight.

The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fleming) says it can only be done by increasing tariffs, and that shows how reactionary' and backward-looking he is. He is living in the nineteenth century. He thinks that these things can only be done in a protectionist economy, but that is not the way it has to be done; that is the not the way it would be done under a Liberal government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: How would it be done?

It could be done by tax incentives; it could be done by a sensible financial policy; it could be done by a sound fiscal policy; it could be done by a government making capital available in a co-operative enterprise with industry; it could be done in a dozen ways without raising tariffs. If the minister does not know anything about that-

-perhaps that is why he was moved into the ministry of justice.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the third point-we have talked about jobs, about industry, about municipal development-is training. Before I say anything about this, and my hon. friends opposite are going to be surprised by this, I want to pay my tribute to what has been done by the government in the field of technical training. However, a great deal more needs to be done than has been done. The thing modern industry increasingly requires is skilled workers. I am sure the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) knows this; that is where the jobs are. It is, even more, where the jobs will be. For this purpose we have to invest more money in human resources. I cannot think of any other way by which we can get a better return from our investment. This means more and better vocational training. I have already paid my tribute to what has been done by the government in this field, and I do not think I need to repeat it. It means better vocational training for young people beginning work and also for the unemployed who need a fresh start, new skills. Perhaps most important of all, we need training for people who are now doing jobs that will decline in the changing years ahead. There should be a retraining program for these workers before, not after, unemployment.
We in the Liberal party, Mr. Speaker, are determined to establish a vigorous agency for job training which will work with industry and with the provinces, which will provide Canadians of all ages with the opportunity to obtain skills for better jobs. While this is important, it has to be backed up by improvement in the opportunities for basic education that the rising generation of Canadians deserve and can achieve. I know this

The Address-Mr. Pearson remains a function of the provinces. No federal government would desire to do anything which would interfere with that responsibility. However, helping the individual to take advantage of education is the concern of all Canadians. Far too many of our boys and girls are leaving school at 16 and drifting into aimless occupations, and many of them should remain at school to go on to university.

You have not done nearly enough about it. I will tell you something more you can do about it, but you won't be given a chance. Family allowances should be extended from age 16 to age 21 for all of those boys and girls who are continuing their education. Our program-

We have already provided, Mr. Speaker, for a system of university scholarships and university loans which will enable every boy and girl in this country to get a university education if he or she can qualify for it, irrespective of his or her financial position. Well, that is one aspect and only one aspect of the Liberal program for growth, for jobs, for progress and for development.
You are advocating bigger deficits or higher taxes.

As I have said, this program will cost money but it will be an investment expenditure which it will be desirable to make. There is also the progress that should be made in the field of social security, arising

out of an expanding and growing economy, and that is towards portable contributory pensions covering everybody.
That is in the speech from the throne.

There is something in the speech from the throne on it and, as could be expected, there is a reference to discussing it at a provincial conference. The government says it will talk about it with the provinces before discharging its responsibility as a federal government; but a pension plan, as such, does not require any further constitutional amendment. It can be drafted by this parliament if any government would take the responsibility for doing it. There is doubt, of course, about widows and orphans benefits, but that need not hold up the main plan, if the government had one. We could go ahead with what we can do and then work out these other points later.
If the government is really determined that existing private pensions should be made portable, it can effectively secure that result by changes in the income tax administration.
I am sure the time has come when we in this country can, and should have, a national pension plan making an adequate and fully portable pension available, on a contributory basis, to every Canadian. That is the Liberal plan which we have worked out in detail and which a new Liberal government will be ready to carry out.
Those, as I see them and as my party sees them, are the five main lines of action we need in Canada today: construction, new industry, training, health, contributory pensions. Those are the main points of a program for Canada, a program which we have put forward and which we will put forward again, and those are the standards by which a party will be judged in the days and weeks ahead. Those are the standards by which this government stands condemned. It offers now, as it provided before, bumbling indecision instead of a plan; palliatives instead of resolute action; restriction instead of expansion, confusion instead of progress.
There is only one very unimportant reference to international affairs in the speech from the throne. There is no indication ot any kind regarding the real seriousness of the international situation. There is a reference to Berlin, and that is about all. There is no indication of how things are really going in the world. True, there is some mention of disarmament, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs keeps working away at disarmament, going up to New York and to Geneva, and then back again. We wish him well and applaud his efforts and his sincerity, but in the speech from the
throne there is practically no indication of what is going on in the world and of the dangers in which we live. There is, of course, a reference to our own position, and it is:
Canada has continued to play an increasingly effective role in international affairs.
If that means that Canada is a country held in high regard for the achievements of its people in peace and war, for its promise of great progress under good government, for what it has done in the past and what it is going to do in the future, then that is good, but, Mr. Speaker, do not confuse it as a reference to the Canadian government. If the government tries to tell us that it has continued to play an increasingly effective role in international affairs, then I would ask it to present the evidence in support of that.
Shame.

There is nothing in the speech from the throne about defence policy, but one would expect that from a government which has no defence policy, and which is spending millions of dollars in ways that really do not add to our defence at all. What we should have had years ago, and what we fought for in this house, is a defence committee on policy where we could try to find out the principles upon which the government is acting in defence matters. We have never been able to do that, but when a Liberal government takes over that will be done. The defence policy will be examined by a committee in the House of Commons in the way it should be examined, in a way it has not been examined since this government took office.
There are other things required for a program of national advancement but, before we can put programs of the kind I have indicated into effect, there must be a re-awareness on the part of government of the needs of the people and the necessity of relating policies to those needs and those feelings. There must be an end to financial mismanagement and a beginning of efficient public administration of our affairs. I do not know if that can begin in the Senate. There must be a tightening of our belts, we are told, but it must be a tightening of the belt by the best method, which is an expansion of the body economic. The purpose of the Liberal policy is to provide for that expansion with increased production and incomes. Government social measures which are necessary can be paid for out of that expansion. That is the only way in which these payments can safely be made.
I know that government intervention these days is increasingly necessary in our huge and complicated society of concentrations of bigness and power; I know that government

The Address-Mr. Pearson must intervene more and more in order to protect the individual. But the object of that intervention must always be protection against those forces which would limit the freedom of the individual and would not itself limit that freedom.
Government should not be a prop. Government should provide the conditions where a man does not need a prop, but can stand on his own feet. Government cannot do everything, and the feeling that it can, and that it should, is one of the greatest threats to our freedom today. That feeling can weaken; it can even destroy our self-reliance, individual and national, by obscuring the necessity for individual and national effort, individual and national service, individual and national sacrifice. If that necessity is not accepted and met by the individual and by the nation, then we are not going to be able to solve our problems as a democracy, however good the programs we may put forward as a government.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this effort, service and sacrifice must be directed to maintaining and strengthening moral values in our society as well as in seeking material progress. If that is not the case, then no government policies, however wise in themselves or however wisely administered, will save us. The challenge in a democracy is ultimately and always to the people, because it is they who have the power and the responsibility, including the choice of those to whom, in parliament and in government, they delegate so much of that power and responsibility.
Mr. Speaker, it would have been encouraging to have found in the speech from the throne some expression of these basic problems; some understanding of these new, deep-seated and massive problems that confront us individually, nationally and internationally. But there was nothing of that in this speech. There was nothing about the real state of the nation; nothing about the test that it now faces within its boundaries and within the world; nothing of the necessity of the right responses to the challenges that are ahead. Instead, Mr. Speaker, this speech gave all the indications of a last minute and scrambling search for anything that might be lying around anywhere to stuff the Christmas stocking. Stuffing the Christmas stocking is not good enough for 1962.
In short, Mr. Speaker, there is nothing in this speech or in the conduct of the government since June 18 that gives us any reason to hope or think that the dreary or confused record of the last five years would be improved if this minority government continued in office.
We have heard a good deal in recent weeks-a good deal more in recent days-

of the necessity of putting the national interest above the playing of politics. That talk does not come very convincingly, to me at least, from those whose concern to avoid an appeal to the people could preserve a state of political weakness and uncertainty such as we have in this parliament today.
I do not believe we will get progressive action and efficient administration, wise, forward-looking, sound policies from a weak and discredited minority government which in the throne speech has shown, as its record has proven, how little it could do to meet the real needs of the Canadian people, the real needs which it does not even understand.
The alternative, Mr. Speaker, is a government with a plan of action of the kind I have indicated and which will be filled in later by my colleagues; a plan which is based upon the principles I have mentioned.
Some people in this house have been building up hopes of a change of heart in the present government. The third and fourth parties seem to be looking for some justification for supporting this minority government, for voting for the ministers and the policies that a few months ago they were very strongly condemning-quite as strongly as we were. I feel that in this respect the throne speech has let them down badly. It is not little, but it is certainly limping and late.
It is going to be very difficult, surely, to find any evidence of real change in the dish of Tory leftovers that the throne speech provides; a change that will mean policies that will put the unemployed to work. This is a speech which includes so much of last year's budget speech of the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Fleming); which includes so much of the last election campaign pronouncements of the government, which were repudiated by the people on June 18; which has added two or three new boards and commissions, including a national economic committee on development. That is a proposal we put forward first in this house in 1958 and subsequently, and it was rejected by the government. It was torn to pieces by the minister of labour in one speech, when he argued that this kind of thing was no good.
Socialist.

He said it was socialist. Of course, I admit that is new; it is new to the government, but not to us. We have been pleading for this for four years.
Also, in the throne speech there is a paragraph that represents one of the most amazing conversions in modern political history, which provides for the arrangements for the export of power from British Columbia to the United States. That, I admit also, is new. But apart from a few things like this

and a board or commission here or there, this speech is a rehash of last year's budget and the last election campaign statements. 1 do not know how anyone can get any hope of a change in the heart and mind of the government from that kind of speech from the throne.
Early this year the government produced another throne speech. Hon. members ought to read it. They will find a lot of this one in it. In those days, Mr. Speaker, this government had a very massive majority in this house, but they got very little done before they dissolved parliament.
You were the reason.
The reason they gave for not getting very much done was that they had been obstructed by a minority.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Forty nine people.

They had 204 and I think we had 49 or 50; but we prevented them doing the things they meant to do. Now they have 116 and the combined opposition is 140 or 150; but they feel sure they can do the things now that they could not do with that great majority. They say, "It is easy now we are in a minority". Obstruction will not matter now. It does not matter that they can be outvoted. They did not do very much to implement the last throne speech, and I do not think we can have very much confidence in the present one.
The third and fourth parties said: we must wait and see; we must wait and see what the government has to propose in the speech from the throne. It may be, they said, it will have some promise of action in it such as would entitle us to declare confidence in this government. Well, they have waited and they have seen, and they have seen what I believed they would see and what I suspect they knew themselves they would see. They have seen a government which is incapable of important new initiative-a government incapable of undertaking new projects; a government pressed by so many conflicting interests that it takes refuge in indecision. Oh, it will do a bit more of some things and a bit less of others, set up councils and repeat the same old stuff. But what is there in this program, in the speech from the throne, which answers the criticisms made by all the opposition parties of this government, criticisms which were on June 18 supported by 63 per cent of the electorate? This program, I repeat, is made up of Tory leftovers from the last parliament.
If you had no confidence in the government in the last parliament, how can you have any confidence in this government now? Is this a parliamentary situation to make you change
The Address-Mr. Pearson your minds? Is this a program to make you change your minds? I do not envy any member of the opposition who has to go to the country to explain why he has now decided that this government which he so recently criticized so strongly has suddenly become a government which should be kept in office. Surely, no one who understands our national problems could vote confidence in this government. The financial editor of the Montreal Gazette, an unimpeachable authority, wrote on August 29-this was after the election:
The government's credits of domestic and international good will are alike just exhausted. It will have to be very convincing in both the scope of its programs and in its determination to see them through to retain its mandate.
I suggest that this government has been convincing in neither the scope of its programs nor in its determination to see anything through, and I hope I have given enough evidence to show why we on this side have no confidence in this administration and why we feel it is not only our duty but our privilege to move a vote of no confidence so that this house may decide whether it wishes the government to carry on or whether it wishes the people to be given a chance to put into office a government which will know how to carry on.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) that the following be added to the address:
We respectfully affirm to Your Excellency that Your Excellency's advisers do not possess the confidence of this house.

What did the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) do-
Defeated the Tory party, that is what he did.

-when he was a minister to achieve this on behalf of the automobile industry? Then there was a major program to help Canadians take full advantage of educational opportunities. In that connection I shall quote the government of the province of Quebec to the effect that such a plan has been in existence in that province which has provided 3,000 jobs. Skills: the only thing in the whole plan to meet the present situation is an increase of family allowances from 16 to 21. Health: how he touched upon this. He has had the experience of Saskatchewan. As a matter of fact, that policy as enunciated today by him in this house represents the antithesis of the stand taken by the Liberal party in the province of Saskatchewan. I point this out, Mr. Speaker, in the best of good spirits: the promise that in 1919, if they ever got back here, they were going to bring that in.

I have read in advance in the press that a broadside would be launched by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). Do you know what it reminded me of? It reminded me of the boy with a number of firecrackers who joined each one together in a number of packages because they took longer to explode and did not do very much harm. I am going to deal, when the opportunity comes, with some of the statements made by him outside of parliament. There was far greater exhibition of vituperation and virulent abuse outside the house than here in parliament, and I will deal with them at length. With the exception of one or two of those matters, his speech seemed to me to be a warmed over election speech, generated in large measure by frustration. This speech reveals the annoyance which must come to those who have almost had the cup in hand, yet find it dashed to the wayside.
I expected a different speech. But I did find one thing. I did find the tremendous interest which he now takes in third parties. He keeps referring to us as a minority government. I think of the references he made to the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) only three or four weeks ago. Possibly he will recall those things. He speaks of us as being a minority, because he says that 63 per cent of the people voted other than for us. For whom did the others vote who did not vote for the Liberal party? Is there a paradox in existence, that if you vote for a third party you are voting against the government but for his opposition?
He talks about minority governments. Here is the record. He says that having 37 per cent of the population for us denies us the right to be the government. Here is the record year by year. In 1921 the Liberal party had 41.5 per cent of the vote. It ruled in this country-and that is the proper expression in the case of that government-for a period of four years. Then he spoke of how Mr. King came before parliament in 1925. He had 40.1 per cent of the vote, and the Conservatives had 46.5 per cent. He said that it was a wonderful thing that they had a fewer number of members in the house than did the Conservative party, by some 11 or 12. And they hung on.
